speeches.Cir:: Dissembling Traytor, now I see the cause, Of all thy fawning, was but to be free: T'was not for nothing, thou hadst teeth and clawes, For thou hast made a cruell prey of me.
speeches.Circe:: And he is gone (aye me) is stolne from hence, And this poore Casket of my breast, hath left Without a Hart: that should for recompence, Haue lockt in two: O most inhumane theft! The Gods, more freedome did allow, when Ioue turn'd Io to a Cow. Man-Maide, bee gone! Cease Dreadfull Ioue! Finding thy Drift, My Bounty, shall prevent thy Guift: This Machles Payre, I make, my Heire: All I possesse, I heere, Resigne, Thou hast 〈…〉 And I haue Mine.
Then take my keyes! and shew me al my wealth. Leade me abroad! Let me my subiects view! Bring me some Physick! though that bring no health! And feyne me pleasures, since I finde none true.
I cannot blame ye if ye gaze, And giue small eare to what I say: For such a presence will amaze, And send the Senses all one way.
How rich is earth? and poore the skies? Depriu'd of heauenly Beauties eyes? Whose Image men adore.
Heroicke Vertue, is that kind Of Beautie, that attracts the mind, And men should most implore.
Ianus was happy that could see, Two wayes at once: And happier he That round about him kept Watches, that neuer slept.
speeches.Cho:: But we most happy, that behold, Two that haue turn'd this Age to Gold, Making old Saturns Reigne, In theirs, come backe againe. And since more, th'obiect, then the sight, Makes euery seer Blest; How are we rauisht with delight, That see the best.
speeches.Cupid:: It is but Iustice, to torment a heart, That tortured thousands: And my gentle reigne, So wrongd with acting of a Tyrants part, I must Restreyne, My powre abus'd; And right my iniurd Treyne. Then was the wound I gaue her deepe.
Thou claim'st her Subiects: And I claime the Soyle, As Soueraigne Lord: The Hecatomes shee brings, Though great Oblations, yet deduc'd from Spoyle, Are sordid Things: And sent of Earth: Vertue pure Incense brings.
speeches.Pallas:: Are mortall Creatures, growne so proud To taxe the Skye, for euery Cloud: Though I could turne thee, to a Stone Ile begge thy peace:
speeches.Iupiter:: Deare Daughter cease! Shee giues but what shee can not keepe.
speeches.Both:: T'was I whose power none can withstand, That open'd both her heart, and hand.
